selected.look_here_first: Start with broad basal leaves, then inspect the tall stalk and clusters of small pale discoid flower heads rather than looking for showy rays.
Look at alternate simple leaves and five-lobed funnel-shaped flowers; check the calyx and stamens instead of judging by flower color.
Look for a basal leaf rosette with densely woolly undersides, slender flowering stalks and nodding composite heads; inspect bracts and mature seed pappus.
Start with the radiating fingerlike terminal grass spikes; examine individual spikelets, their awns and the fertile floret to distinguish related Chloris.
Look closely at hairy, often lobed leaves and stems; examine the tiny clustered flowers and their bracts rather than relying on growth habit alone.
Look for a low creeping mat with small kidney-shaped leaves on long stalks, then inspect the tiny solitary flowers and developing fruits beneath the leaves.
Inspect the triangular sedge stems and umbrella-like clusters of flattened spikelets subtended by leaflike bracts; use mature achenes for confirmation.
Look for opposite leaves on branching stems, milky sap and extremely small cyathia; examine the cyathial glands and three-lobed capsules.
Start with small opposite leaves and aromatic square stems; examine the hairy flower calyx and two-lipped corolla for comparison with other Hedeoma.
Inspect very small opposite leaves on four-angled aromatic stems, then use the tubular calyx and small bilabiate flowers for identification.
Look for alternate leaves with prominent veins from near the blade base, short axillary flowers and a small capsule; compare bud and twig details.
Look for finely divided foliage and compound umbels of tiny pale flowers; inspect mature hairy fruits and leaf-sheath bases to separate parsley-family look-alikes.
